subject: Efficient parameterization of a mixture of a truncated & unconstrained negative binomial distribut.

messages.author: 3f37be0cf708d442
messages.subject: Efficient parameterization of a mixture of a truncated & unconstrained negative binomial distribut.
parts:
Hello,

Related to other discussions about the negative binomial on the list, I’d be glad if I could get some feedback about the efficient parameterization of a mixture of a truncated and unconstrained negative binomial (NB) distribution.

Personally I find working with means and variances easiest, but there is no neg_binomial_cdf_2_log or neg_binomial_ccdf_2_log in stan (at least it is not mentioned in the manual), so it looks as if one has to use the “standard” parameterization with alpha and beta for truncated NB distributions.

 

The data I want to model are best described as a combination of 150 data points from a negative binomial with alpha = 35, beta = 3 plus 1050 data points from the same distribution with a lower truncation point at its 90th percentile (i.e. I know the mixing proportions).

 

For the first model, B, I directly parameterized the NB with alpha and beta. This does not work well; I stopped waiting for it to converge after a couple of minutes (all models are below).

 

The second model, B, is based on a model I found on the Stan mailing list and is parameterized through alpha and mu, so that beta is calculated as mu/alpha. This makes it easier (for me) to define reasonable priors. But this model still needed 100+ seconds to complete 1000 iterations (including warm up) and also resulted in only around 100 n_eff.*

 

So, while model B seems to works, I believe that I must be overlooking something important here. In particular, I am surprised by how much slower the negative binomial is compared to a similar model using normal distributions: When I simulate similar data from a constrained and unconstrained normal distribution and estimate the parameters with the corresponding Stan model, everything is done in 4.5s!

 

My concrete questions are:

Is this speed-difference between the normal and negative binomial to be expected?

If no, what would be alternative ways to improve the efficiency of the model?

(It would be great if any suggestions would also generalize to an NB regression, which is what I ultimately want to do and where I assume not to be able to use very informative priors)

 

 

Best - Guido

 

################################# MODEL A ################################

data {

  int<lower=1> K;      // number of mixture components

  int<lower=1> N;      // number of data points

  int y[N];           // observations

  simplex[K] theta;    // mixing proportions

  int L;              // cutoff, lower bound for truncated distribution

}

 

parameters {

  real<lower=0.1, upper=50> alpha;    // alpha (shape) parameter of negative binomial

  real<lower=0, upper=20> beta; // beta (in scale) parameter of negative binomial

}

 

model {

  alpha ~ cauchy(0,10);

  beta ~ cauchy(0,5);

  for (n in 1:N) {

    if (y[n] < L){

       increment_log_prob(log(theta[1]) + neg_binomial_log(y[n],alpha,beta));}

    else {

        increment_log_prob(log_sum_exp(log(theta[1])

                                        + neg_binomial_log(y[n],alpha,beta),

                                      log(theta[2])

                                        + neg_binomial_log(y[n],alpha,beta)

                                        - neg_binomial_ccdf_log(L,alpha,beta)));}

  }

}

 

################################# MODEL B ################################

# note: without data block, which is the same as for model A

parameters {

  real<lower=0.1, upper=50> alpha;    // alpha (shape) parameter of negative binomial

  real<lower=0, upper=30> mu; // mean of negative binomial distribution

}

 

transformed parameters {

  real<lower=0> beta;

  beta <- alpha/mu;

}

 

model {

  alpha ~ cauchy(0,5);

  mu ~ cauchy(0,5);

  for (n in 1:N) {

    if (y[n] < L){

       increment_log_prob(log(theta[1]) + neg_binomial_log(y[n],alpha,beta));}

    else {

        increment_log_prob(log_sum_exp(log(theta[1])

                                        + neg_binomial_log(y[n],alpha,beta),

                                      log(theta[2])

                                        + neg_binomial_log(y[n],alpha,beta)

                                        - neg_binomial_ccdf_log(L,alpha,beta)));}

  }

}

 

* I also briefly thought about a model that directly parameterizes with mu and sigma, whereby alpha = mu^2/(sigma-mu) as well as beta = mu/(sigma-mu) are defined in the transformed parameters block. But this won’t work because the denominator mu-sigma becomes easily negative, if one does not define mu and sigma so that sigma is always greater than mu, and I hope there are better ways to formulate the model.

messages.author: 8aa9b8cc06fdc99c
messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] Efficient parameterization of a mixture of a truncated & unconstrained negative binomial distribut.
parts:
Negative binomial is a lot harder to compute on the log scale.
It involves gamma functions for the binomial coefficient and
two logarithms, and most of these don't have shared computations
for vectorization. In the normal, you have to compute log sigma,
but you only need to do that once for multiple y and/or mu.

But it's the sampling efficiency that's more worrying and also
more difficult to diagnose. We've started playing with some negative
binomials to implement the Zheng et al. paper:

http://www.stat.columbia.edu/~gelman/research/published/overdisp_final.pdf

but I still don't have a good feel for the sampling difficulties.

If things aren't mixing well, you can try turning down the initial step
size or upping the target acceptance rate, both of which should help, but
slow things down (it's the latest trick I learned from Michael, so sorry
for suggesting it everywhere now). You may also want to run more warmup
iterations. If that doesn't help with n_eff per iteration,
then you need to look at identifiability in the model more closely.

We should add the CDFs for neg_binomial_2, but that won't happen until Stan 2.6
at the earliest. I created an issue:

https://github.com/stan-dev/stan/issues/1129

(I assigned it to Marco, who implemented neg_binomial_2, but I don't know
if he'll have time to get to it any time soon --- Marco, feel free to unassign
yourself.

I haven't thought through changes of variables for CDFs. Michael's the one to ask
for help, since he implemented most of the other CDFs and is just generally awesome
at calc.)

- Bob

messages.author: 146bc26797d1c5e2
messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] Efficient parameterization of a mixture of a truncated & unconstrained negative binomial distribut.
parts:
I fitted a negative binomial model last weekend, and noticed that prior for phi of neg_binomial_2 made a big difference. I didn't found a good prior for phi itself, but (half-)normal(0, s)  as a prior for 1/phi works well, at least when s=1. From mvcv I knew that phi would be around 4–10. 

Also tried individual-level normal and cauchy random effects, for the data has some large residuals, but these were too slow.

(BTW, I wouldn't mind if Stan had beta-binomial and dirichlet-multinomial built in. I needed to code the latter manually yesterday. These distributions are a bit like negative binomial in the sense that they handle the overdispersion of count data, and are faster than leaving the intermediate individual-level "random effects" to be sampled.)

messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] Efficient parameterization of a mixture of a truncated & unconstrained negative binomial distribut.
parts:
Thanks for chiming in.

I'd like to add that if you have:

parameters {
real<lower=0> phi;
...
model {
1 / phi ~ normal(0,1)

then the non-linear change of variables means you need to add the
Jacobian correction

log | d/d.phi (1 / phi) |

to the log density if you want phi to have the right distribution:

increment_log_prob(pow(phi,-2));

Beta binomial is built in as beta_binomial.

dirichlet_multinomial isn't built in yet, but we should definitely include
it. I created the feature request:

https://github.com/stan-dev/stan/issues/1130

On the topic of multinomials, we also need to work on K-1 parameter versions
that implicitly apply the K-1 version of softmax (one input constrained to 0),
and there's already an issue for that:

https://github.com/stan-dev/stan/issues/266

- Bob

We have to get more serious

messages.author: 8aa9b8cc06fdc99c
messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] Efficient parameterization of a mixture of a truncated & unconstrained negative binomial distribut.
parts:
I got the sign right, but forgot the log! There's an absolute value.
The Jacobian adjustment on the log scale adds

log | d/du f(u) |

= log | d/du u^(-1) |

= log | - u^(-2) |

= log | u^(-2) |

= log ( u^(-2) )

= -2 * log(abs(u))

so you want

increment_log_prob(-2 * log(abs(u)));

That last abs() is to account for

u^(-2) = (1 / u^2)

being positive by by construction.

- Bob
